h: How the router processes an ACL
t: Top-down, first match. The router reads the ACEs in order and stops at the first one that matches . Later lines are never checked, so put specific lines above general ones. The implicit deny. Every ACL ends with an invisible deny any (standard) or deny ip any any (extended). If nothing matches, the packet is dropped. An ACL with only deny lines blocks everything . Sequence numbers. ACEs are numbered 10, 20, 30… In a named ACL (or ip access-list standard 10 ) you can insert 15 deny … between two lines, remove one with no 20 , and renumber with ip access-list resequence . Typing no access-list 10 deletes the whole numbered list. The three Ps.…

Standard → close to the DESTINATION It can only see the source address. Put it near the source and it would block that source from everywhere, not just the network you meant to protect. ip access-group 10 out on the interface facing the protected LAN. Extended → close to the SOURCE It can match the exact destination and service, so drop unwanted traffic as early as possible and don't waste bandwidth carrying it across the network. ip access-group NAME in on the interface where the traffic arrives.

A wildcard mask tells the router which bits to check. 0 = must match , 1 = ignore . For a subnet, wildcard = 255.255.255.255 − subnet mask . Type an address and a wildcard, or pick an example. Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is a database of every user, computer and group in an organisation, held on servers called domain controllers (DCs). A Group Policy Object (GPO) is a bundle of settings. It does nothing until it is linked to a site, the domain or an OU. Computer Configuration applies to computers in that OU at start-up; User Configuration applies to users in that OU at log-on. If two GPOs configure the same setting, the one applied last wins — so the OU closest to the object usually wins. Single packets you send that match a test also update it. # From → To Service Expected Actual 1 PC-A → Public web site HTTPS (tcp 443) Allowed — 2 Internet user → Web server HTTPS (tcp 443) Allowed — 3 Internet user → Web server SSH (tcp 22) Denied — 4 Internet user → PC-A RDP (tcp 3389) Denied — 5 PC-A → Public web site Ping (ICMP echo) Allowed — Copy test log

Every ASA interface has a security level from 0–100. The number says how trusted the network behind it is. 100 Inside your LAN — most trusted 50 DMZ public-facing servers 0 Outside the internet — least trusted

Higher → lower is allowed. Traffic starting on a more-trusted interface can reach a less-trusted one (Inside → Outside, Inside → DMZ, DMZ → Outside) with no rule needed. Lower → higher is denied. A new connection from a less-trusted interface to a more-trusted one is blocked by default (Outside → Inside, Outside → DMZ, DMZ → Inside). Stateful inspection. The ASA remembers connections it allowed out, so the reply traffic is let back in automatically — you don't write a rule for return traffic. An ACL makes the exceptions. Disk 1 4 TB SAS Online Disk 2 4 TB SAS Online Disk 3 4 TB SAS Online Disk 4 4 TB SAS Online

Level Usable (4 × 4 TB) Failures survived RAID 0 (striping) 16 TB 0 RAID 1 (mirror, 2 disks) 4 TB 1 RAID 5 (striping + parity) 12 TB 1 RAID 6 (double parity) 8 TB 2 RAID 10 (mirrored stripes) 8 TB 1 (sometimes 2) RAID keeps the server running when a disk dies. It is not a backup : deleted or encrypted files are deleted or encrypted on every disk at once.

RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) spreads data across several disks so the server keeps running when one dies. It protects against hardware failure only. Level How Usable (4 × 4 TB) Survives RAID 0 Striping, no copy 16 TB Nothing RAID 1 Mirror of 2 disks 4 TB 1 disk RAID 5 Striping + 1 parity 12 TB 1 disk RAID 6 Striping + 2 parity 8 TB Any 2 disks RAID 10 Mirrored pairs, striped 8 TB 1 (2 if in different pairs) Ransomware, accidental deletion and fire hit every disk in the array at once. That is what backups are for.
Backup speed and size Restore Full Slowest, biggest Fastest: one set Incremental Fastest, smallest Slowest: full + every incremental since Differential Grows each day Full + the newest differential

Keep 3 copies of your data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy off-site. Many organisations add a copy that is offline or immutable (it cannot be changed), so ransomware cannot encrypt it too. Off-site copies holding personal data must be encrypted under UK GDPR, and kept only as long as your retention policy says.

Recovery Point Objective (RPO) : how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. Nightly backups mean up to 24 hours of work could be lost. Recovery Time Objective (RTO) : how long you can be down while you restore. Tape and cloud restores are slower than a local NAS. A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup. Test restores regularly and check the files open.

An Ethernet cable holds 8 copper wires in 4 twisted pairs (orange, green, blue, brown). Each pair is twisted at a different rate. Twisting makes interference hit both wires equally, so it cancels out at the receiver, and it reduces crosstalk between pairs.  Type Shielding Use it… U/UTP None (unshielded) Offices and homes. Cheap, flexible, and the most common. F/UTP, S/FTP (STP) Foil around the cable and/or each pair, plus a drain wire Near motors, lifts, welding gear or fluorescent ballasts (high EMI). Must be earthed at the panel.

The category says how fast a signal the cable can carry (its bandwidth in MHz). The standard copper channel limit is 100 m . A public subnet has a route to the internet gateway; a private one does not. Availability zones are separate data centres in one region: put copies of important servers in two zones so one failure does not take the service down.

Each VM has a firewall group (some providers call it a security group). Inbound traffic is blocked unless a rule allows it by port and source . Using another group as the source means "only from my web servers", which keeps working when their addresses change. Never open SSH (22) or RDP (3389) to 0.0.0.0/0. Bots scan the whole internet for them within minutes.

Give each person their own account in a group with least privilege , and turn on MFA , above all for admins. Keep buckets private and encrypted ; turn on versioning to undo deletions. Cloud is pay-as-you-go, so set a budget alert and switch off what you do not need.

PBKDF2 repeats a hash many thousands of times. One login takes milliseconds, but an attacker making billions of guesses is slowed down by the same factor. (bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2 do the same job.) Password Iterations: 96,000 Derive key (PBKDF2-SHA-256) Derived hash —

An attacker can hash millions of common passwords once , in advance, and store a lookup table of hash → password (a "rainbow table" is a compact version). With plain hashes, every stolen hash can be looked up instantly, and identical passwords stand out. hash("Summer2026!") = 8f1c… found in table ✔ → hash("x7Qp… " + "Summer2026!") = 2be0… not in any table ✘ A salt is a random value, unique to each user, stored next to the hash. It is not secret . Because every user's input is different, a table made in advance is useless, and the attacker must start again for every single account. Same password, different salt → completely different hash.…

t: 0NF Unnormalised: repeating groups — several values crammed into one row (like the lines on an order slip). 1NF Every cell holds one value, no repeating groups, and every row has a primary key. 2NF 1NF, and no partial dependencies: every non-key column depends on the whole key. 3NF 2NF, and no transitive dependencies: non-key columns depend on nothing but the key. “The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.” 1NF needs a key · 2NF: the whole key · 3NF: nothing but the key.

An arrow means “determines”: if you know the value at the tail, there is only one possible value at the head. Arrows from part of the key are partial dependencies; arrows from a non-key column are transitive.

Wildcard masks are the inverse of the subnet mask: /24 = 0.0.0.255, /30 = 0.0.0.3. network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0 turns OSPF on for any interface in that range. h: How does it decide something is an attack?

Layer 3 — Network Joins different networks together and forwards packets between them, choosing the best path using IP addresses and its routing table.
Layer 2 — Data Link Connects devices on the same LAN and sends each frame only out of the port where the destination MAC address is, using its MAC address table.
Layers 2 & 3 A LAN switch that can also route between VLANs and subnets at high speed, combining Layer 2 switching with Layer 3 routing in one box.
Layer 1 — Physical A basic device that repeats every incoming signal out of all its other ports, so every connected device shares one collision domain.
Layers 3–7 (security) Sits between trusted and untrusted zones and permits or blocks traffic by checking it against a set of security rules.
Layers 1 & 2 Lets Wi-Fi devices join a wired network by sending and receiving radio signals and bridging that traffic onto the LAN.
End device (Layers 1–7) Provides services or shared resources — such as web pages, files, email, DHCP or DNS — to client devices across the network.
End device (Layers 1–7) A fixed end device used by a person at a desk; it sends and receives data, usually through a wired network interface card.
End device (Layers 1–7) A portable, battery-powered end device that normally connects using Wi-Fi but can also use a wired port.
End device (Layers 1–7) An end device that carries voice calls as data packets over the network (VoIP), often powered through the cable by PoE.
End device (Layers 1–7) A shared output device with its own IP address, so many users can send jobs to it over the network.
WAN Represents networks outside your control — the Internet or a wide area network — usually reached through an ISP.

Find the smallest block where block size − 2 ≥ hosts needed: 8 − 2 = 6 (too small), 16 − 2 = 14 ✓. A block of 16 = 24, so 4 host bits and 32 − 4 = /28 . Mask: 256 − 16 = 240 → 255.255.255.240 . h: How to work out a subnet (worked example)
t: Example (not one of your answers): a subnet that needs 12 hosts, starting at 10.0.0.0 . Find the smallest block where block size − 2 ≥ hosts needed: 8 − 2 = 6 (too small), 16 − 2 = 14 ✓. A block of 16 = 24, so 4 host bits and 32 − 4 = /28 . Mask: 256 − 16 = 240 → 255.255.255.240 . Network 10.0.0.0 · first usable 10.0.0.1 (the gateway) · last usable 10.0.0.14 · broadcast 10.0.0.15 · 14 usable hosts. The next subnet starts at 10.0.0.16 . Tip: allocate the largest subnet first so every subnet lands on a boundary. Prefix → block size: /24 = 256 · /25 = 128 · /26 = 64 · /27 = 32 · /28 = 16 · /29 = 8 · /30 = 4.

h: Firmware: UEFI, Secure Boot and TPM
t: UEFI replaced the old BIOS. It boots from the EFI System Partition on a GPT disk and keeps a list of boot entries (Windows Boot Manager, ubuntu…). Legacy / CSM mode pretends to be an old BIOS. A disk installed in UEFI mode will not boot in Legacy mode. Secure Boot only runs boot loaders signed by trusted keys. Windows and Ubuntu are both signed. TPM 2.0 stores encryption keys (BitLocker, Windows Hello). Most PCs have it in the CPU as fTPM or PTT, but it may be turned off. Windows 11 needs: UEFI with Secure Boot capability, TPM 2.0, 4 GB RAM, 64 GB storage and a supported 64-bit CPU.

Each channel is a separate 64-bit path to the CPU. Two sticks on different channels (A + B) can be read at the same time — dual channel doubles the bandwidth. Two sticks on the same channel (A1 + A2) run in single channel . With two sticks the manual says A2 and B2 : the slots at the end of each channel's wiring give the cleanest signal.

Size it: add up the CPU TDP + GPU power + about 50 W for the board, RAM and fans, then add 30% headroom for power spikes and to keep the PSU near its efficient middle range. e.g. 65 W CPU + 115 W GPU + 50 W = 230 W → 230 × 1.3 = 299 W minimum 80 PLUS rating Efficiency at 50% load* White (standard) 80% Bronze 85% Silver 88% Gold 90% Platinum 92% Titanium 94% *Figures for 115 V; on 230 V UK mains they are slightly higher. The wasted power becomes heat — a 90% PSU delivering 450 W draws 500 W from the wall.

Electrostatic discharge (ESD) — you can carry thousands of volts without feeling it; under ~3 000 V you won't feel a spark, but chips can be damaged by far less. Wear an anti-static wrist strap clipped to bare, unpainted metal on the case, and work on an anti-static mat. Handle cards and sticks by the edges ; never touch the gold contacts or the CPU pins. Keep parts in their anti-static bags until needed. Unplug mains / switch the PSU to O before working inside. Never open a PSU — its capacitors hold a charge. The strap has a 1 MΩ resistor so a mains fault can't send a large current through you — but still take it off before connecting mains.

One flag doesn't prove phishing; three or four together nearly always do. Slow down when you see them. The name doesn't match the address. The display name is just text. "Helen Marsh (CEO)" at freemail.example is not your CEO. Look-alike or cousin domains. oakfie1d.test (digit 1), 0akfield.test (zero), brightwatter.test (extra t), oakfield-hr.example (extra word). The link text lies. Hover (don't click) and read the real destination in the status bar. The text can say anything, even a genuine-looking URL. Asks for a password, code or "re-validation". IT never needs your password by email. Go to known sites by typing the address yourself.…

h: SPF, DKIM and DMARC in one picture
t: Result What it tells you spf=pass The sending IP is allowed to send for the envelope (Return-Path) domain. spf=softfail / fail The IP is not on the list: a strong sign of a forged sender. dkim=pass d=… Signed by that domain and not changed in transit. Check that d= matches From. dmarc=fail Nothing lined up with the From domain. With p=none the mail is still delivered. Passing isn't the same as safe. A look-alike domain (oakfie1d.test ) or a webmail account passes all three, because the attacker owns it. The checks prove which domain sent it, not whether that domain is honest.

h: Read a link from the right
t: The registered domain is the part just before the ending. Everything to its left is a sub-domain, which the owner can set to anything. https:// password.oakfield.test. account-verify.example /reset?id=j.reid Owned by account-verify.example . "password.oakfield.test" is just a sub-domain they created to fool you. https:// learning. oakfield.test /course/sec-2026 Owned by oakfield.test , the genuine domain.

File Why it's risky invoice.pdf.exe Windows hides the real .exe ; it's a program. .docm / .xlsm Macro documents: "Enable Content" runs code. .zip / .iso Hide the real file from email filters. .js / .htm / .html Scripts or fake sign-in pages that open in a browser.

Don't click, reply, forward to colleagues or open attachments. Press Report phishing on the ribbon. It sends the full message, with headers , to the security team and removes it from your inbox. A routing table doesn't store single addresses — it stores whole networks . Read each entry left to right: S 192.168.1.128/26 [1/0] via 10.0.0.6, Gi0/1 S — code letter How the route was added (not how good it is). 192.168.1.128 — network ID The network this entry represents. /26 — subnet mask How many bits are the network part (255.255.255.192). [1/0] — admin distance / metric Trust in the source / cost of the route. via 10.0.0.6 — next hop The IP of the next router to send the packet to. Gi0/1 — interface The router's own port the packet leaves by.

C Directly connected — the router reaches it through its own interface, so no next hop . L Local — the interface's own exact address (/32). S Static — typed in by an administrator with ip route . O OSPF — learned dynamically from an OSPF neighbour. R RIP — learned dynamically via RIP. D EIGRP — learned dynamically via EIGRP. S* Candidate default — a static default route. * The route currently chosen as the default.

To forward a packet, the router compares its destination IP against the network ID + mask of every entry, then applies these rules in order: 1. Longest prefix match. If more than one entry matches, the router uses the one with the longest (most specific) mask — e.g. a /26 beats a /24 for the same address. 2. Administrative distance. If it learned the same network from two sources, it trusts the lower AD — e.g. a static route (AD 1) is preferred over OSPF (AD 110). 3. The default route (0.0.0.0/0). Matches everything, but only wins when nothing more specific matches — normally the way out to the internet. No match at all? With no default…

h: Static vs dynamic — the difference the exam asks for
t: Static routes are added by hand (ip route … ) and never change unless edited — simple, secure, predictable, good for small networks. Dynamic routes are built automatically by a protocol (RIP/OSPF/EIGRP) and update themselves when links change — better for large, growing networks, but need more processing and care. The code letter tells you how a route was added, not how good it is.

A hypervisor lets one physical computer (the host ) run several virtual machines (the guests ). Each VM has its own virtual CPU, memory, disk and network card, and runs its own operating system. Type 1 hypervisors run straight on the hardware, so they are faster and used in servers and data centres. Type 2 hypervisors are apps on a normal operating system: easy for labs and testing. Hyper-V on Windows 11 is actually type 1: once it is on, Windows itself runs on top of the hypervisor. The CPU must support virtualisation (Intel VT-x or AMD AMD-V ) and it must be enabled in the UEFI firmware .

A Virtual Private Network builds an encrypted tunnel across the internet, so private office addresses can talk as if they were on one network. Anyone capturing the traffic in between sees only scrambled data between the two public IP addresses. Type Joins Example Site-to-site Two whole networks, firewall to firewall Head office ↔ branch, always on Remote access One device to a network A home worker's laptop, connected when needed

Phase 1 settings must match exactly on both ends: IKE version, encryption, hash, Diffie-Hellman group and the pre-shared key (or certificates). Phase 2 says which traffic is protected: each side's local network is the other side's remote network, like a mirror.

Setting Avoid Use IKE IKEv1 IKEv2 Encryption DES, 3DES AES-256, AES-GCM Integrity MD5, SHA-1 SHA-256 or better DH group 1, 2, 5 14, 19, 20 Perfect forward secrecy (PFS) makes fresh keys for each phase 2 session, so one stolen key does not unlock old traffic.

Split tunnel : only traffic for the office goes through the VPN. Faster, less load on head office, but home web browsing is not filtered. Full tunnel : everything goes through head office, so the company web filter and logging protect it too. The address pool gives each VPN client an address. It must not overlap the office networks or common home networks such as 192.168.1.0/24, or the laptop cannot tell which side an address is on. Always add multi-factor authentication : stolen VPN passwords are one of the commonest ways attackers get into a network.

The router address a device sends traffic to when the destination is on a different network. Without one, a PC can only talk to devices on its own subnet.
A logical address that identifies a device on a network, such as 192.168.1.10. It is made of a network part and a host part, split by the subnet mask.
Shows which part of an IP address is the network and which part is the host. 255.255.255.0 (/24) means the first three octets are the network.
Splitting one network into smaller networks by borrowing host bits. It reduces broadcast traffic, separates departments and saves addresses.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing: writing the mask as a slash number, e.g. /24 = 255.255.255.0, /26 = 255.255.255.192.
A 48-bit hardware address burned into a network card, written like 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. Switches use MAC addresses to forward frames within a LAN.
A Layer 2 device that learns which MAC address is on which port and forwards each frame only to the right port. Each port is its own collision domain.
A Layer 3 device that joins different networks and forwards packets between them using IP addresses and a routing table. It is the default gateway for its LANs.
A Layer 1 device that repeats every signal out of every other port. All devices share one collision domain, so it is slow and insecure. Switches replaced hubs.

h: Difference between a switch and a router
t: A switch connects devices within one network using MAC addresses (Layer 2). A router connects different networks together using IP addresses (Layer 3).
A device that connects wireless clients to a wired network. It broadcasts an SSID and applies wireless security such as WPA2 or WPA3.
The name of a wireless network. Hiding the SSID is not real security: the name is still sent when devices connect.
The newest Wi-Fi security standard. WPA3-Personal uses SAE instead of a pre-shared key handshake, which protects against offline password guessing. Older devices may only support WPA2.
Wi-Fi security using AES encryption. WPA2-Personal uses a pre-shared key (password); WPA2-Enterprise logs each user in through a RADIUS server.
An old Wi-Fi encryption method that can be cracked in minutes. Never use it.
An access point setting that only lets listed MAC addresses connect. It adds a layer of control but is weak on its own, because MAC addresses can be spoofed.
A Virtual LAN splits one physical switch into separate broadcast domains, e.g. VLAN 10 for staff and VLAN 20 for students. Devices in different VLANs need a router to talk.
A switch port that carries traffic for many VLANs between switches or to a router, tagging each frame with its VLAN number (802.1Q).
A switch port that belongs to one VLAN, used for end devices such as PCs and printers.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: a server that hands out IP addresses, masks, gateways and DNS servers to devices automatically.
Domain Name System: turns names like www.example.test into IP addresses, like a phone book for the internet.
Network Address Translation: lets many private addresses share one public IP address when they go out to the internet.
A test that sends ICMP echo requests to an address and waits for replies. It shows whether a device can be reached and how long it takes.
Address Resolution Protocol: finds the MAC address that belongs to an IP address on the local network.
A seven-layer model of how networks work: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Use it to troubleshoot from the bottom up.
Transmission Control Protocol (Layer 4): reliable, connection-based. It uses a three-way handshake and resends lost data. Used for web pages, email and file transfers.
User Datagram Protocol (Layer 4): fast and connectionless with no resending. Used for streaming, voice calls, gaming and DNS.
Hardware or software that allows or blocks traffic using rules. Stateful firewalls remember outgoing connections and let the replies back in.
An ordered list of permit and deny rules on a router or firewall. It is read top to bottom, the first match wins, and there is a hidden deny at the end.
A separate network for servers the public must reach, such as a web server, so that the internal LAN stays protected.
An Intrusion Detection System watches traffic and raises alerts. An Intrusion Prevention System sits in the path of the traffic and can block attacks as well.
Security Information and Event Management: collects logs from many systems in one place so analysts can search them and spot attacks.
Emails or messages that pretend to be from someone trusted to trick you into clicking a link, opening an attachment or giving away passwords.
Scrambling data with a key so only someone with the right key can read it. Symmetric uses one shared key; asymmetric uses a public and a private key.
A one-way function that turns data into a fixed-length value. Used to store passwords and check files have not changed. You cannot reverse a hash.
The Windows Server directory service that stores users, computers and groups in a domain and controls who can log in and what they can access.
Settings applied by Active Directory to users or computers in an OU, e.g. password rules, mapped drives or blocking Control Panel.
A folder in Active Directory used to organise users and computers so policies and permissions can be applied to them.
The column (or columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table. It can never be blank or repeated.
A column that holds the primary key of another table. It is how tables link together.
Organising tables to remove repeated data and anomalies: 1NF (one value per cell), 2NF (no partial dependencies), 3NF (no transitive dependencies).
An Entity Relationship Diagram shows the tables (entities), their keys and how they relate, with the cardinality at each end.
How many rows on one side of a relationship can link to rows on the other: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.
Structured Query Language: used to create tables (CREATE TABLE), add data (INSERT) and search it (SELECT ... WHERE).
A step-by-step set of instructions to solve a problem. Show it as a flowchart or as pseudocode before you write code.
Structured English that describes an algorithm without worrying about a language’s exact syntax.
A Python library for working with tables of data (DataFrames): read a CSV, clean it, filter it, group it and summarise it.
A Python library for drawing graphs. Always give a graph a title and axis labels.

The processor: it fetches, decodes and executes instructions. Speed depends on clock speed, number of cores and cache.
Fast, temporary memory holding the programs and data in use. It is volatile: it is cleared when the power goes off.
The main circuit board that connects the CPU, RAM, storage and expansion cards. Its socket and chipset decide which parts are compatible.

Straight-through cables join different devices (PC to switch). Crossover cables join similar devices (switch to switch), though most modern ports auto-detect. Cat 6 supports 1 Gbps (10 Gbps over short runs).
The two wiring standards for RJ45 plugs. Use the same standard at both ends for a straight-through cable, and one of each for a crossover.
Every device connects to a central switch. If one cable fails only that device is affected; if the switch fails, everything stops.
The Windows command line. Useful commands: ipconfig, ping, tracert, nslookup, netstat.
The Windows command shell and scripting language. Commands are verb-noun cmdlets such as Get-Service or New-ADUser.
Read (r), write (w) and execute (x) for the owner, group and others, e.g. chmod 754 file.
